faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is the "Retail Market" that these documents keep referring to?
faqs.answer: The Retail Market is the part of the Philippine electricity industry where large electricity users ("Eligible End-users") can choose their own electricity supplier instead of automatically buying power from their local Distribution Utility (DU). It exists alongside the traditional "Captive Market," where customers have no choice of supplier and are served only by their DU.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What does RCOA stand for and what does it do?
faqs.answer: RCOA stands for Retail Competition and Open Access. It is the policy, mandated by Section 31 of the EPIRA (Republic Act No. 9136), that allows qualified electricity end-users to buy power from a supplier of their choice and to use the distribution/transmission wires of the local network provider under "open access," instead of being locked into their franchised utility.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is the Omnibus Rules for Customer Choice Programs in the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: It is a single, consolidated regulation issued by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) through Resolution No. 13, Series of 2024, dated 14 August 2024. It merges and updates the previously separate rules governing RCOA/CREM, the Green Energy Option Program (GEOP), and the Retail Aggregation Program (RAP) into one rulebook.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Why did the ERC consolidate all these rules into one Omnibus document?
faqs.answer: Before 2024, the rules on contestability, RES licensing, switching, SOLR, and GEOP were scattered across many separate resolutions issued between 2005 and 2022. The ERC combined them to remove inconsistencies, close implementation gaps (such as disputes over Fuel Cost Recovery Adjustments), streamline license applications, and strengthen consumer protection against abuse of market power.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is EPIRA and why does it matter to the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: EPIRA is Republic Act No. 9136, the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001. It restructured the Philippine power industry into generation, transmission, distribution, and supply segments and created the legal basis for retail competition (Section 31) and the ERC's regulatory authority (Sections 2 and 43).

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What are the three Customer Choice Programs available in the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: The three programs are: (a) the Competitive Retail Electricity Market (CREM), often called RCOA; (b) the Green Energy Option Program (GEOP), which lets end-users source 100% renewable energy; and (c) the Retail Aggregation Program (RAP), which lets smaller end-users pool their demand to qualify for the Retail Market.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Is joining the Retail Market mandatory for a qualified customer?
faqs.answer: No. Module A4.2 of the Omnibus Rules expressly states that participation in any of the Customer Choice Programs is voluntary. A customer that qualifies may choose to remain a captive customer of its DU if it prefers.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Who are the main players regulated under the Omnibus Rules?
faqs.answer: The Omnibus Rules apply to Retail Customers, Retail Suppliers, Suppliers of Last Resort (SOLR), Network Service Providers (NSP), Retail Metering Service Providers (RMSP), the Central Registration Body (CRB), and Eligible End-users.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is a "Captive Customer" versus a "Retail Customer"?
faqs.answer: A Captive Customer is an end-user who has no choice of electricity supplier and is served only by its franchised DU at ERC-regulated rates. A Retail Customer is an Eligible End-user who has exercised its choice and entered into a Retail Supply Contract (RSC) with a licensed Retail Supplier.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What government agency regulates the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) is the primary regulator, mandated under EPIRA to promulgate rules, issue licenses, resolve disputes, and enforce compliance. The Department of Energy (DOE) also plays a role, particularly for GEOP thresholds and market commercial-operations declarations.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is the Central Registration Body (CRB) and why is it important to a beginner?
faqs.answer: The CRB is the entity designated (through the Market Operator) to manage the systems and processes that handle customer switching, registration, and information exchange in the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM) and Retail Market. Virtually every switch, disconnection, or reconnection request passes through the CRB.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM) and how does it relate to retail supply?
faqs.answer: The WESM is the market established under Section 30 of EPIRA where generation and other market participants trade electricity. Retail Suppliers that source power from the WESM must register as WESM members and comply with WESM Rules, including prudential (financial) requirements.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What historical milestones led to today's lower eligibility thresholds?
faqs.answer: RCOA started in 2013 in Luzon and Visayas at a 1 MW threshold. It dropped to 750 kW in 2016, then to 500 kW under Resolution No. 12, Series of 2020. Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 further lowers it to 100 kW effective 26 June 2026, aligning CREM/RAP with the existing GEOP threshold.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is a "threshold" in the context of the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: The threshold is the minimum average monthly peak demand (measured in kilowatts, kW) that an end-user must reach to be considered "eligible" to participate in a Customer Choice Program. Different programs can have different thresholds, though the Omnibus Rules and Resolution No. 22 are aligning them at 100 kW.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Where can a beginner find official information about switching suppliers?
faqs.answer: The ERC operates the "Buy Your Electricity" website (bye.erc.ph), which Network Service Providers must reference in the eligibility notice printed on a customer's monthly bill, together with the ERC's official website for the list of licensed suppliers.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is a Network Service Provider (NSP)?
faqs.answer: An NSP is an entity that owns, controls, and operates a transmission or distribution system — typically the local Distribution Utility (DU) or, for directly connected customers, the National Transmission Corporation (TransCo) or its concessionaire (currently the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines).

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What does "Open Access" actually mean in practice?
faqs.answer: Open Access means any qualified person may use the transmission and/or distribution wires and associated facilities of the network, upon payment of ERC-approved wheeling rates, regardless of who supplies them with electricity. It separates the "wires" business from the "supply" business.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is the difference between a DU and a Retail Supplier?
faqs.answer: A Distribution Utility (DU) owns and operates the wires (the distribution network) within its exclusive franchise area and is heavily regulated. A Retail Supplier (RES, Local RES, or RE Supplier) sells electricity itself and competes for customers; it does not own the wires but pays the DU/NSP wheeling charges to deliver power to its customers.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Can a DU also act as a Retail Supplier?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only through its unbundled, non-regulated retail arm called a Local Retail Electricity Supplier (Local RES), which operates only within the DU's own franchise area under a Letter-authority rather than a full RES License, and subject to strict business-separation rules to prevent cross-subsidy and preferential treatment.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What is a Directly Connected Customer (DCC)?
faqs.answer: A DCC is an industrial or bulk electricity end-user supplied directly through the transmission grid or sub-transmission assets still owned by TransCo, rather than through a DU's distribution system. Once a DCC's demand meets the CREM eligibility threshold, it is treated as a Retail Customer.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: What happens to the household consumer eventually under this framework?
faqs.answer: EPIRA envisions that the contestability threshold will keep falling until it reaches household demand levels, meaning ordinary residential consumers will eventually also gain the right to choose their electricity supplier, similar to reforms already implemented for large industrial and commercial users.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Are these rules the same in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao?
faqs.answer: The general framework is the same nationwide, but implementation dates differ. Mindanao's WESM went commercial only in January 2023, and RCOA/GEOP in Mindanao formally launched on 26 March 2024 per DOE Department Circular No. DC2024-03-0009, several years after Luzon and Visayas.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Does the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (BARMM) follow these same rules?
faqs.answer: Under Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 (paragraph 6), implementation of all Customer Choice Programs in BARMM is left to the authority and discretion of the BARMM government, rather than being automatically imposed by the ERC.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Who actually approved and signed the Omnibus Rules?
faqs.answer: The Omnibus Rules were adopted through ERC Resolution No. 13, Series of 2024 ("A Resolution Adopting the Omnibus Rules for Customer Choice Programs in the Retail Market"), following Focus Group Discussions in May-June 2023 and public consultations in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao in December 2023.

faqs.section_title: Getting Started — Understanding the Retail Electricity Market
faqs.question: Why is understanding this framework valuable, even for a total beginner?
faqs.answer: Electricity is typically one of the largest recurring costs for commercial and industrial operations. Understanding how to exercise supplier choice, how switching works, what protections exist, and what obligations apply can materially affect a company's electricity costs, contract risk, and regulatory compliance. 2. Key Terms and Definitions

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Retail Supply Contract (RSC)?
faqs.answer: An RSC is the contract entered into by a Retail Customer and its chosen Retail Electricity Supplier (or Local RES) that sets out the price, terms, and conditions under which electricity will be supplied — essentially the core legal document of the customer-supplier relationship.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is the difference between "Contract Price" and "Electricity Price"?
faqs.answer: The Contract Price is the rate agreed between the Retail Customer and Retail Supplier for energy consumption, excluding pass-through and other related charges. The Electricity Price is the total amount billed, which includes the Contract Price plus pass-through charges and other ERC-approved charges.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What are "Pass-Through Charges"?
faqs.answer: These are amounts collected by the Retail Supplier from the Retail Customer that are not the supplier's own revenue but are simply passed on to other parties — mainly NSP (distribution/transmission) charges and other ERC-approved charges such as Universal Charge and FIT-All.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Cooling-off Period?
faqs.answer: It is a period of five (5) business days (or longer, if agreed) starting from the signing of the RSC, during which the Retail Customer has the right to cancel the contract without penalty, unless the customer validly waives this right.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What does "Switching" mean under the Omnibus Rules?
faqs.answer: Switching is the commercial transfer of a Retail Customer from the NSP (as regulated supplier) to a Retail Supplier or SOLR, or from one supplier to another. It takes effect on a regular meter reading date, or a special meter reading date following a Last Resort Supply Event.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is the difference between an "Initial Switch" and a "Regular Switch"?
faqs.answer: An Initial Switch is the very first transfer of a customer from the NSP's regulated service to a Retail Supplier. A Regular Switch is any subsequent transfer from one Retail Supplier to another (or to a SOLR) after that initial switch.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a "Last Resort Supply Event" (LRSE)?
faqs.answer: An LRSE is any of several specified circumstances (listed in Module G3.2) — such as contract termination, a supplier ceasing operations, or license revocation — that trigger a Retail Customer's need to switch to a Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR) or another Retail Supplier.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)?
faqs.answer: A SOLR is a regulated entity — either a DU or a licensed RES with an ERC-approved Business Separation and Unbundling Plan — designated by the ERC to provide temporary "backstop" electricity supply to a Retail Customer following an LRSE, until the customer secures a new Retail Supplier.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is an Eligible End-user?
faqs.answer: An Eligible End-user is an end-user that has met the ERC's (or DOE's, for GEOP) demand eligibility threshold, as evidenced by a single revenue meter, giving it the right (though not the obligation) to switch to the Retail Market.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is meant by an "Aggregated Group" and "Aggregated Member"?
faqs.answer: An Aggregated Group is a set of End-users whose individual demand has been pooled together by a Retail Supplier to collectively meet the eligibility threshold for contestability under the Retail Aggregation Program. Each individual end-user within that pooled group is called an Aggregated Member.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Central Registration Body (CRB) and what does "CRB" actually do administratively?
faqs.answer: The CRB manages the required systems, processes, and IT platforms — including the Central Registration and Settlement System (CRSS) — that handle customer switching, registration, and information exchange, and it is the hub through which most notices between suppliers, NSPs, and customers are routed.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Distribution Wheeling Service Agreement (DWSA)?
faqs.answer: A DWSA is the agreement between a DU and a Retail Supplier (in a single billing scheme) — or between a DU and a Retail Customer (in a dual billing scheme, or when the customer is under SOLR) — that covers the procurement of Distribution Wheeling Service (DWS), i.e., the use of the distribution wires.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Connection Agreement (CA)?
faqs.answer: A CA is the agreement between a Connection Customer and a DU that governs the distribution connection assets and services at a customer's premises — essentially the technical/physical hookup contract, separate from the commercial supply contract.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Metering Services Agreement (MSA)?
faqs.answer: An MSA defines the responsibilities of the Retail Metering Service Provider (RMSP) and the End-user regarding the provision of metering facilities, equipment, and services, consistent with the Omnibus Rules, DSOAR, the Philippine Distribution Code, OATS Rules, the Grid Code, and WESM Rules.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a Transmission Services Agreement (TSA)?
faqs.answer: A TSA is the agreement between the Transmission Provider and a user of transmission facilities (e.g., a Directly Connected Customer or its Retail Supplier) specifying the terms of transmission service; it also functions as the Connection Agreement for transmission-connected customers.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is meant by a "Primary Retail Supplier"?
faqs.answer: When a Retail Customer has multiple Retail Suppliers, it must nominate one, in writing, as its Primary Retail Supplier — the single point of contact with the CRB and NSPs, responsible for billing/collecting all NSP charges and for executing the DWSA with the DU.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a "Prudential Requirement"?
faqs.answer: It is the financial safeguard amount that a WESM Trading Participant (including Retail Suppliers) must maintain to guarantee it will meet its payment obligations under the WESM Rules; the CRB verifies compliance with this requirement before approving a switch request.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What does "Reversion" mean?
faqs.answer: Reversion is the event where a Retail Customer or Aggregated Member/Group returns from the Retail Market back to the Captive Market — typically triggered by a sustained drop in average monthly peak demand below a specified percentage of the applicable threshold.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a "CREM End-user Redistributor"?
faqs.answer: This is a CREM End-user (such as a building owner, mall operator, or homeowners' association) that has switched to CREM through a single revenue meter and then redistributes the electricity it purchases to individual sub-metered occupants, such as condominium unit owners or mall tenants.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is the "Bill Deposit" and how is it different from the "Cash Security Deposit"?
faqs.answer: A Bill Deposit is what a DU collects from a new or additional customer, equal to about one month's estimated billing, to guarantee payment while still a captive customer. A Cash Security Deposit is a similar guarantee collected by a Retail Supplier or SOLR, but it must be held in an escrow, restricted account, or Hold-out Agreement facility, unavailable for the supplier's working capital.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a "Hold-out Agreement"?
faqs.answer: It is an arrangement where a cash security deposit is held subject to bank-placed and/or customer-placed restrictions, ensuring the deposit is preserved and cannot simply be spent by the Retail Supplier or SOLR that collected it.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is meant by "Tangible Net Worth" (TNW), and why does it matter to license applicants?
faqs.answer: TNW is the value of all of a company's assets, excluding intangible assets and goodwill, minus its liabilities. RES License applicants must show a TNW of at least PhP15,000,000 (or their Average Expected Annual Expenses, whichever is higher) to demonstrate financial capability.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is the "Average Expected Annual Expenses" (AEAE) formula used for RES applications?
faqs.answer: AEAE is computed as the sum of Total Cost of Sales (TCOS) plus Total Operating Expenses (TOE) expected over the license term, divided by the term of the license. It sets the minimum financial-capability bar an applicant must meet or exceed with its Tangible Net Worth.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What does "Contiguous Area" mean for aggregation purposes?
faqs.answer: It refers to end-users located within defined common boundaries — such as a subdivision, village, economic zone, business district, condominium, or shared franchise area — whose electricity supply can be individually metered even though their demand is pooled together under the RAP.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a "Virtual Meter"?
faqs.answer: A Virtual Meter is a mathematical model that uses process conditions to estimate flow rates instead of relying on one physical meter; it is used to create a calculated meter point by combining readings from one or more physical meters, often used for Aggregated Groups.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is meant by "Pilferage" under these Rules?
faqs.answer: Pilferage refers to the unauthorized taking or use of electricity, including tampering with meters, bypassing meters, or otherwise obtaining or consuming electricity without proper authorization or payment — it is expressly prohibited for all Retail Customers.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is the "GEOP Operating Permit"?
faqs.answer: It is a document issued by the DOE to an entity, allowing it to supply electricity to a GEOP End-user, pursuant to DOE Department Circular No. DC2020-04-0009 (Guidelines for the Issuance of Operating Permits for RE Suppliers under GEOP).

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is meant by "Letter-authority" versus "RES License"?
faqs.answer: A RES License is the ERC authorization issued to a standard Retail Electricity Supplier. A Letter-authority is a similar but distinct authorization issued to a Local RES (i.e., a DU's in-franchise retail arm or a Special Economic Zone operator) in lieu of a full license, since it operates only within a defined area.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a "Letter of Designation"?
faqs.answer: It is the document issued by the ERC to a Retail Supplier or DU authorizing it specifically to act as a Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR), separate from its regular RES License or franchise.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What does "No Disturbance Request" mean for a customer?
faqs.answer: It is a formal request made by an Eligible End-user or Retail Customer asking that it not be contacted again for marketing purposes by a Retail Supplier; once made, the request must be respected at all times unless the customer revokes it.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is a "Marketing Contact"?
faqs.answer: A Marketing Contact is any contact — in person, by phone, or through written or electronic communication — made by a Retail Supplier with a Retail Customer for the purpose of promoting or inviting the customer to enter (or consider entering) into an RSC.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What does "Business Separation and Unbundling Plan" (BSUP) mean?
faqs.answer: A BSUP is the ERC-approved plan under which a DU or Retail Supplier structurally and functionally separates its regulated distribution/regulated supply business from its non-regulated supply or SOLR business, ensuring there is no cross-subsidy between the two.

faqs.section_title: Key Terms and Definitions
faqs.question: What is meant by "Affiliate" under the Omnibus Rules?
faqs.answer: An Affiliate is any person that, alone or with others, directly or indirectly controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with another person — including parent companies and subsidiaries — relevant to ownership-limitation and anti-cross-subsidy rules for Retail Suppliers. 3. Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Who needs a RES License to operate in the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: Any person or entity that wants to sell, broker, market, or aggregate electricity to End-users in the Retail Market must first secure a RES License (or a Letter-authority, if it qualifies as a Local RES) from the ERC. Operating without one is prohibited and subject to sanctions.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Who is exempt from securing a full RES License?
faqs.answer: Two categories are exempt but still need ERC authorization in the form of a Letter-authority: (a) Distribution Utilities acting as Local RES within their own Franchise Areas, and (b) persons/entities authorized to supply electricity within their respective Special Economic Zones.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Who is eligible to apply for a RES License in the first place?
faqs.answer: Three types of entities may apply: (a) a natural person of legal age or juridical person registered with the DTI as engaged in retail electricity supply; (b) a juridical person registered with the SEC for that business; and (c) an entity created by law whose charter allows it to generate its own revenues.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: How long does the ERC take to process a RES License application?
faqs.answer: The ERC must approve or deny a complete application within sixty (60) calendar days from the issuance of the ERC docket number, pursuant to Republic Act No. 11234 (the EVOSS Act) and other applicable laws.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What are the three broad categories of requirements for a new RES License application?
faqs.answer: Applicants must submit (a) Legal Requirements proving identity and authority to do business, (b) Technical and Managerial Capability Requirements proving they can run a supply business, and (c) Financial Capability Requirements proving they can sustain the business.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What legal documents must a new RES applicant submit?
faqs.answer: These include a duly accomplished RES Information Sheet; SEC Certificate of Registration and Articles of Incorporation/Partnership (or DTI Business Name Registration for sole proprietorships, or the applicant's charter if created by law); a valid Business/Mayor's Permit; and Audited Financial Statements for the two most recent periods (or Audited Interim Financial Statements if under two years old).

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What if the applicant is also engaged in the generation business?
faqs.answer: It must submit proof of filing its Business Separation and Unbundling Plan (BSUP) application and Accounting Separation Statements reflecting separate capitalization for its RES business, ensuring the generation and retail-supply activities are not commingled.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What experience must an applicant's staff have to prove "technical and managerial capability"?
faqs.answer: Either (a) at least two managerial employees/officers with a combined ten years of relevant experience, including at least one with experience negotiating with the System Operator, DU, or Generation Companies; or (b) an engaged consultant with at least fifteen years of relevant experience, paired with at least one employee/officer having similar negotiation experience.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What other technical/managerial documents are required besides staff experience?
faqs.answer: An organizational chart with CVs of the Board and Officers; proof of an approved CRB sign-up account; proof of adopting a billing and collection system; proof of an existing or developing company website; a Five-Year Business Plan with financial projections (RES Form 3); and a Five-Year Staffing and Training Plan.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What financial capability must a new RES applicant demonstrate?
faqs.answer: A Tangible Net Worth of at least PhP15,000,000 or its Average Expected Annual Expenses (AEAE), whichever is higher, evidenced by Audited Financial Statements (or Audited Interim Financial Statements for newer companies), or proof of TNW for newly incorporated applicants yet to commence operations.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What is a Market Risk Management Plan and why must an applicant submit one?
faqs.answer: It is a plan showing the measures the applicant will take to mitigate exposure to price volatility in procuring power supply for retail — required so the ERC can assess whether the applicant can withstand market disturbances that could threaten its ability to serve customers.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What must an applicant commit to regarding unhedged contracts?
faqs.answer: It must submit a Sworn Undertaking to, at minimum, post a Performance Bond for every unhedged Retail Supply Contract, or otherwise document hedging instruments as evidence of its ability to withstand market disturbances or cost-increasing events.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier collect cash security deposits from its customers?
faqs.answer: Only if it declared its intention to do so during licensing and can present a certification from a Philippine financial institution confirming it has an escrow, restricted account, or Hold-out Agreement facility for that purpose. Suppliers that did not declare this intent may not collect cash security deposits during their license validity.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What documents are needed to renew a RES License?
faqs.answer: Similar categories apply: an updated RES Information Sheet, valid Business/Mayor's Permit, proof of BSUP status (if applicable), AFS for the two most recent periods, latest General Information Sheet, updated Business Plan and financial projections, updated organizational chart, proof of an active website, and updated financial-capability documents (TNW/AEAE, Market Risk Management Plan, Performance Bond proof).

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: When must a RES apply for license renewal?
faqs.answer: Not later than sixty (60) calendar days before the expiration of its current license, submitting all required documents as Certified True Copies of the originals.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What happens if a Retail Supplier previously submitted a required document to the ERC?
faqs.answer: It may submit a Sworn Statement of Prior Submission in lieu of resubmitting the same document, stating what was submitted, when, to which ERC office, and confirming there have been no amendments since. The ERC may still require resubmission if it cannot verify the document in its records.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What extra requirements apply specifically to a Local RES application?
faqs.answer: A Local RES must submit a Local RES Information Sheet; for private corporations, the GIS of the applicant and its affiliates in generation/distribution/retail supply; for electric cooperatives, a Board Resolution or Secretary's Certificate listing the Board; an organizational chart; AFS/AIFS; ERC-approved BSUP Application; latest Accounting Separation Statements; and a Five-Year Business Plan.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Does an RE Supplier under GEOP need anything in addition to a RES License?
faqs.answer: Yes. An RE Supplier must also secure an Operating Permit from the DOE pursuant to DOE Department Circulars DC2018-07-0019 and DC2020-04-0009, on top of its RES License or Letter-authority from the ERC.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: On what grounds can the ERC suspend or revoke a RES License or Letter-authority?
faqs.answer: Grounds include providing false or misleading information; bankruptcy, insolvency, or being at fault in a Last Resort Supply Event; failing to serve any customer within two years of licensure without justifiable cause; failing to maintain a satisfactory Good Standing rating; engaging in anti-competitive behavior or abuse of market power; and other violations of applicable laws or ERC issuances.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What are the core ongoing obligations of every licensed Retail Supplier?
faqs.answer: These include maintaining functional/structural unbundling if also in other electricity businesses; keeping an ERC/DOE-linked website with indicative prices; using the CRB's Central Registration and Settlement System for switching; unbundling bill components; complying with financial-capability standards; and properly segregating any cash security deposits collected.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: How must a Retail Supplier treat cash security deposits it collects?
faqs.answer: They must be held in an escrow, restricted account, or Hold-out Agreement facility, unavailable for the supplier's working capital, and the supplier must pay the customer annual interest equivalent to the deposit's actual interest earnings, applied as a bill deduction.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier draw on a customer's cash security deposit?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only if the customer breaches its payment obligations, and only under terms agreed by both parties. Conversely, if the supplier fails to deliver supply, it must refund the deposit plus interest earned, less any outstanding obligations.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What ownership restrictions exist between Retail Suppliers and the Independent Market Operator (IMO)?
faqs.answer: A Retail Supplier, its Affiliates, or any of its stockholders, directors, officers, or relatives within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity, may not hold any direct or indirect interest in the Independent Market Operator.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What cross-ownership restriction applies between Retail Suppliers and TransCo?
faqs.answer: A Retail Supplier or its stockholders/directors/officers (and their spouses, within the fourth civil degree) may not hold shares in TransCo or its buyer/concessionaire, subject to narrow exceptions for small (1% or less) holdings of publicly listed shares with no other economic relationship.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Is there a limit on how much power a Retail Supplier can buy from its own affiliated generators?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Retail Supplier may not purchase more than fifty percent (50%) of its capacity requirements from its affiliate Generation Companies, to prevent excessive self-dealing and preserve competitive sourcing.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What fees does a RES License applicant pay, and when?
faqs.answer: A PhP10,000 application fee is paid upon issuance of the ERC's Confirmation of Completeness Email (CCE). If approved, the applicant then pays a PhP100,000 RES License fee upon issuance of the Notice of Approval (NOA), to facilitate release of the license. These fees may change under the ERC's Schedule of Fees and Charges.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: How long is a new RES License valid, and how long can renewals last?
faqs.answer: A new RES License is valid for five (5) years. On renewal, a supplier rated "Very Satisfactory" under the Good Standing scorecard gets a ten (10)-year renewal, while a "Satisfactory" rating gets a five (5)-year renewal.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What must a Retail Supplier do if it wants to stop operating?
faqs.answer: It must notify the ERC at least sixty (60) calendar days before ceasing operations, provide proof it has refunded any monies owed to Retail Customers, and show a settlement plan or proof of payment to any DU, TransCo, WESM, or Generation Company it owes. Its RES License is then deemed revoked.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What happens if a Retail Supplier defaults and causes an LRSE?
faqs.answer: It remains responsible for continuously supplying electricity to the affected Retail Customer until that customer secures a new Retail Supplier or SOLR. If the new rate is higher than the old contract rate, the customer may seek indemnification through remedies stated in its RSC.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Must a Retail Supplier report material changes in its business to the ERC?
faqs.answer: Yes — any material change to information submitted in its licensing documents (Modules C5 to C7) must be reported to the ERC within three (3) calendar days from the occurrence of the change.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Does the DU's Local RES need to comply with the same 50% net income sharing rule as the DU itself?
faqs.answer: Yes — per Section 26 of EPIRA and its IRR, a DU (including through its Local RES) engaging in business undertakings that maximize asset utilization must apportion at least fifty percent (50%) of the resulting net income to reduce its distribution wheeling charges.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: Can a company holding a RES License also act as a Retail Aggregator or RE Supplier?
faqs.answer: Yes. Any entity with a valid, existing RES License may also operate as a Retail Aggregator and RE Supplier (the latter subject to holding a valid DOE Operating Permit). A Local RES with a valid Letter-authority may also act as an Aggregator, but only with prior ERC approval.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: What generation companies must eventually secure a RES License under the transitory rules?
faqs.answer: All Generation Companies supplying electricity to Directly Connected Customers (DCCs) must secure a RES License within one (1) year from the effectivity of the Omnibus Rules.

faqs.section_title: Becoming a Licensed Retail Electricity Supplier (RES)
faqs.question: How is a Retail Supplier's license term determined for pending applications filed before the Omnibus Rules took effect?
faqs.answer: All pending RES License applications, including renewals, continue to be governed by the existing licensing requirements under ERC Resolution No. 01, Series of 2011, and are issued a five (5)-year license upon approval, pending full transition to the new Scorecard-based renewal terms. 4. Eligibility and Participation of End-Users

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: What are the three ways an Eligible End-user may participate in the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: It may switch to and avail of the Competitive Retail Electricity Market Program (CREM), the Green Energy Option Program (GEOP), and/or the Retail Aggregation Program (RAP), subject to meeting the eligibility requirements of each program.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: What was the CREM/RAP demand threshold under the original Omnibus Rules (2024)?
faqs.answer: 500 kW average monthly peak demand, with the ERC committing to issue separate resolutions progressively lowering the threshold until it reaches household demand levels — which it has since done via Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 (100 kW effective 26 June 2026).

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: How is CREM eligibility determined for an existing end-user?
faqs.answer: Through a Single Revenue Meter showing either (a) a registered historical average monthly peak demand equal to or above the prevailing CREM threshold for the preceding twelve (12) months, or (b) a forecasted average monthly peak demand meeting or exceeding the threshold for the next twelve (12) consecutive months based on load profiling.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: What is the GEOP eligibility threshold?
faqs.answer: An end-user with an average monthly peak demand of 100 kW or more for the past twelve (12) months may participate in GEOP, per DOE Department Circular No. 2018-07-0019.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: How does a newly connected end-user (less than 12 months old) qualify for GEOP?
faqs.answer: Either (a) its estimated average monthly peak demand for the next twelve months, based on load profiling, is 300 kW or above; or (b) its estimate is 100 kW to below 300 kW, and it has a registered historical monthly peak demand of at least 100 kW for three consecutive months.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Can an end-user below 100 kW ever join GEOP?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only after the DOE — in consultation with the ERC, the National Renewable Energy Board (NREB), and industry stakeholders — determines that the necessary technical requirements and standards have been met.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: What is required for a group of small end-users to qualify for the Retail Aggregation Program (RAP)?
faqs.answer: Their aggregated average monthly peak demand for the preceding three (3) months must equal or exceed the prevailing CREM threshold, and the members must be located within a Contiguous Area (e.g., subdivisions, villages, business districts, special economic zones, condominiums, or the same DU franchise area under common ownership or franchise).

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Is there a cap on how many end-users can form an Aggregated Group?
faqs.answer: No — there is no limit on the number of participating end-users, provided their combined aggregated demand meets the prevailing threshold and they are located within a qualifying Contiguous Area.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: How is demand computed for an end-user whose meter cannot record demand directly?
faqs.answer: Demand (kW) equals [(Average Consumption ÷ Number of Days in a Month) ÷ 24 Hours] divided by the applicable Load Factor, where Average Consumption is the average kWh consumption for the preceding three months and Load Factor is as determined by the relevant DU.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Who is responsible for verifying an end-user's computed demand for RAP eligibility?
faqs.answer: The Retail Supplier is responsible for vetting the computed demand, with the assistance of the DU.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: How does an end-user learn that it has become eligible for CREM or GEOP?
faqs.answer: Instead of a Certificate of Contestability, the NSP's monthly billing statement itself serves as proof of eligibility. The NSP must include a specific notice on the bill stating the customer's average monthly peak demand and directing it to the ERC's "Buy Your Electricity" website (bye.erc.ph) for switching details.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Who informs Directly Connected Customers (DCCs) of their eligibility?
faqs.answer: TransCo (or its buyer/concessionaire) is responsible for informing end-users directly connected to transmission and sub-transmission facilities of their eligibility, and for providing the ERC relevant information about them.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Who is the default Retail Metering Service Provider (RMSP) in the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: The DU serves as the default RMSP until the ERC adopts rules authorizing other RMSPs; TransCo (or its buyer/concessionaire) is the default RMSP for Directly Connected Retail Customers.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Who pays for the metering facilities needed to switch to the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: The Eligible End-user bears the cost of appropriate metering facilities and their installation, payable upon execution (or amendment) of a Connection Agreement, plus ongoing ERC-approved metering charges based on its customer classification.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: How long does the RMSP have to install or upgrade metering facilities after a switch notice?
faqs.answer: Thirty (30) calendar days from receipt of the Eligible End-user's notice of intention to switch — extendable up to sixty (60) calendar days for Aggregated Groups.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Can an Eligible End-user own its own electricity meter and pick its own vendor?
faqs.answer: Yes — End-users and Retail Customers have the right to own metering equipment and select their own contractor or vendor, provided the equipment meets the metering requirements under the Philippine Distribution Code, Grid Code, DSOAR, OATS Rules, and AMI Rules, and remains accessible to the RMSP, NSP, or Retail Supplier.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: What rules govern metering standards generally?
faqs.answer: The Philippine Distribution Code (PDC), Philippine Grid Code (PGC), Distribution Services and Open Access Rules (DSOAR), Open Access Transmission Service (OATS) Rules, and the Rules Governing Implementation of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI), among other ERC issuances.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Can a captive customer previously classified as residential now be charged different metering fees after switching?
faqs.answer: In the interim, a customer previously classified as residential under the Captive Market pays the metering charge applicable to low-voltage customers (or the private DU equivalent) until the ERC issues a resolution rationalizing metering costs, but no costs of the Retail Customer's metering may be cross-subsidized by, or charged to, Captive Customers.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Does participating in the Retail Market disqualify an end-user from other demand programs?
faqs.answer: Under Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025, a Retail Customer cannot simultaneously participate under the same Customer Account Number or Meter Service Identification Number in both a Customer Choice Program and other ERC demand-management programs such as Net-Metering or the Distributed Energy Resource (DER) Program.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Is participation eligibility permanent once achieved?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily — a customer's eligibility is based on ongoing demand levels. If a CREM or GEOP customer's demand falls sustainedly below a set percentage of the threshold, it may become eligible to revert to the Captive Market under Module K.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: What is the difference between eligibility for CREM and eligibility for RAP?
faqs.answer: CREM eligibility is based on an individual end-user's own average monthly peak demand meeting the threshold on its own. RAP eligibility is based on the combined, pooled demand of multiple smaller end-users (an Aggregated Group) collectively meeting that same threshold.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Can a DCC continue sourcing power directly from a generation company instead of switching?
faqs.answer: Yes — a DCC may continue directly sourcing power from a generation company until its existing supply contract expires. After that, if its demand meets the CREM threshold, it is treated as a Retail Customer subject to the Retail Market rules.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Are there any restrictions on which type of location may aggregate demand under RAP?
faqs.answer: Aggregation is allowed within subdivisions, villages, business districts, special economic zones, condominium buildings, commercial establishments, mixed-use developments, or the same DU franchise area (if metering facilities belong to the same owner or businesses under the same franchise), or other locations the ERC determines.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: Does an Aggregated Group need to execute one contract or many?
faqs.answer: The Retail Supplier may execute a single RSC covering the entire Aggregated Group's requirements, or, if the Aggregated Members prefer individual contracts, it may enter into separate contracts with each member — provided all contracts carry the same terms and conditions.

faqs.section_title: Eligibility and Participation of End-Users
faqs.question: What must happen before an End-user's participation choice under the Customer Choice Programs becomes effective?
faqs.answer: The applicable eligibility requirements under Modules D2 to D4 must be met, the NSP or DU must confirm the end-user's demand data, and the switching procedures and required contracts under Module E must be completed before the switch date. 5. The Switching Process, Step by Step

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What four initial conditions must be satisfied before a Retail Supplier can submit a switch request?
faqs.answer: (a) an executed RSC between the Eligible End-user and Retail Supplier; (b) an executed DWSA/TSA between the Retail Supplier and NSP (for single billing); (c) an executed Connection Agreement with the NSP and Metering Services Agreement with the RMSP; and (d) expiry of the agreed Cooling-off Period.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: Can a customer with an outstanding balance switch to the Retail Market for the first time?
faqs.answer: No — an Eligible End-user cannot make an Initial Switch while it has an outstanding balance with its NSP. However, upon migrating to CREM/GEOP, it is entitled to a refund of its bill deposit from the NSP.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: Can a customer switch suppliers even if it has a billing dispute with its current supplier?
faqs.answer: Yes, for a Regular Switch — a Retail Customer may switch to a new Retail Supplier or SOLR despite a dispute over billed amounts or undisclosed impositions, though it remains responsible for its other lawful obligations and any remedies the current supplier is entitled to enforce under the RSC.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How long does a Retail Customer have to get its security deposit back after switching away?
faqs.answer: Within thirty (30) calendar days after termination of the RSC, unless a shorter period was agreed in writing by the parties.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How far in advance must an end-user notify its NSP before an initial switch?
faqs.answer: At least ninety (90) calendar days before the intended switch date, via registered mail, electronic mail, or personal service, with the notification actually received by the NSP.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: When must an Eligible End-user provide its Metering Services Agreement (MSA) to the CRB?
faqs.answer: At least thirty (30) calendar days before the intended switch date, providing a signed copy to both the CRB and the Retail Supplier.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What happens if a Retail Customer's bill deposit is insufficient to cover an outstanding balance after an initial switch?
faqs.answer: The Retail Customer must settle the deficit within seven (7) business days of receiving the bill, unless the billing is disputed, in which case it is treated like a captive-customer dispute under DSOAR and related ERC issuances.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What must a Retail Supplier do to notify the NSP and CRB of a new customer relationship?
faqs.answer: It must notify the NSP and CRB (through email, registered mail, personal service, or their platforms) of the required RSC information at least thirty (30) calendar days before the intended switch date.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How much advance notice must a Retail Supplier give the DU when forming an Aggregated Group?
faqs.answer: At least ninety (90) calendar days before the intended switch date, ensuring the DU actually receives the notification that an Aggregated Group has been formed.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: When must a Retail Supplier execute its DWSA or TSA with the relevant NSP?
faqs.answer: At least twenty (20) calendar days before the intended switch date.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What confidentiality obligation applies to customer information a Retail Supplier receives during switching?
faqs.answer: It must be kept confidential in accordance with the Data Privacy Act of 2012, its IRR, and other National Privacy Commission issuances.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What must a Network Service Provider (NSP) do upon receiving a switch notice?
faqs.answer: Enter into a DWSA/TSA with Retail Suppliers fairly and transparently; inform the Retail Supplier of unbundled transmission/distribution charges; maintain authorized meters properly; and submit necessary switching information (including attestations of no outstanding balance) to the CRB within thirty (30) calendar days of receiving the switch notice.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What three separate contracts/attestations must typically be executed for a switch to proceed?
faqs.answer: (a) the RSC between the Retail Supplier and Retail Customer; (b) the wheeling/transmission agreement between the Retail Supplier and the relevant NSP; and (c) the metering services agreement between the Retail Supplier (or customer) and the registered RMSP.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How far ahead of the switch date must a Switch Request be filed with the CRB?
faqs.answer: At least thirty (30) calendar days before the intended switch date, in accordance with the CRB's prescribed manner of submission, copy furnished to the NSP.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What does the CRB check when it receives a Switch Request?
faqs.answer: It verifies whether the Retail Supplier has satisfied its WESM Prudential Requirements (as confirmed by the Market Operator) and checks completeness of the submitted documentation, including verification of the Retail Customer's information from the NSP.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How long does the CRB have to check completeness of a Switch Request and flag any deficiencies?
faqs.answer: Not more than three (3) business days from submission.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What happens if the CRB finds deficiencies in a Switch Request?
faqs.answer: It notifies the Eligible End-user/Retail Customer, the new Retail Supplier, the relevant NSP, and the RMSP of the reasons, and the responsible party (Retail Supplier, RMSP, or the party with a Prudential Requirement shortfall) must rectify the deficiency.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How much time does a party have to correct a deficiency once notified by the CRB?
faqs.answer: Five (5) business days from receipt of the CRB's notice; the maximum seven (7)-day evaluation period is tolled while awaiting the fix. If the deficiency remains unfixed after five days, the CRB notifies all parties that the request will not be processed (without prejudice to refiling).

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How long does the CRB have to approve a complete Switch Request?
faqs.answer: Not more than seven (7) business days from submission of the complete requirements, after which the CRB notifies the Retail Supplier, Retail Customer, RMSP, relevant NSP, and (for Regular Switches) the current supplier/SOLR of the approval and the effective switch date.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What happens if the CRB itself fails to meet the switching timelines?
faqs.answer: Failure to comply with the prescribed periods is a ground for filing a complaint against the CRB.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What must a customer do to relocate within the same DU franchise area and keep the same Retail Supplier?
faqs.answer: Send a Request for Relocation of Service to the Retail Supplier (copy to the CRB) at least thirty (30) calendar days before the planned relocation, stating the new address and intended transfer date, after confirming the new site is within the DU's franchise area with completed connection/metering requirements.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: How quickly must the Retail Supplier respond to a relocation request?
faqs.answer: Within one (1) business day of receipt, indicating whether it will continue or discontinue service at the new location (with reasons if discontinuing), and forwarding a copy to the CRB.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What is the notification chain if the Retail Supplier agrees to continue service after relocation?
faqs.answer: The CRB forwards the request to the DU within one business day; the DU approves/disapproves within two business days; the CRB relays this within one business day; and if approved, the Retail Supplier must sign a new or amended DWSA with the DU within three business days.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What happens if a Retail Supplier does not want to continue serving a relocating customer?
faqs.answer: The Retail Customer must switch to a new Retail Supplier under the regular switching procedure (Module E6) before relocating; if it fails to do so, the CRB notifies the current Retail Supplier and the DU/NSP, and the customer must secure a new RES before being connected at the new site.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What happens if a Retail Customer relocates to a different DU's Franchise Area entirely?
faqs.answer: It is governed by the procedures for new applications under the Omnibus Rules — essentially treated like an entirely new customer relationship rather than a simple relocation.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier transfer a customer's contract to another supplier without the customer's consent?
faqs.answer: No — this is a "Prohibited Commercial Transfer." A Retail Customer cannot be transferred to another Retail Supplier, have its RSC assigned, or be reverted to a non-retail supplier without its written authorization and consent; violations may be the subject of an ERC complaint.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What is the general obligation of an Eligible End-user regarding outstanding balances before switching?
faqs.answer: It must settle all outstanding balances with its current NSP (for initial switches) or comply with its other RSC obligations (for regular switches to another Retail Supplier), even while a billing dispute over specific charges may still be pending.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: Do the switching timelines under Module E also apply to Retail Aggregation switches?
faqs.answer: Yes — Module E2.1's obligations for Eligible End-users apply equally to eligible DCCs and to members forming an Aggregated Group switching under RAP.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: What role does the Market Operator (MO) play in the switching process?
faqs.answer: The MO confirms whether a Retail Supplier's WESM Prudential Requirements are fully satisfied; if not, the CRB will not approve the switch request until the deficiency is resolved to the MO's satisfaction.

faqs.section_title: The Switching Process, Step by Step
faqs.question: Who ultimately decides the effective switch date?
faqs.answer: The CRB, upon completing its evaluation of a complete Switch Request, notifies all relevant parties of the approval and the effective switch date, which is generally tied to a regular (or special) meter reading date. 6. Billing and Payments

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What must a Retail Supplier's bill contain, at minimum?
faqs.answer: Enough information for the customer to verify its charges — kWh usage for the billing period, billing due date, fuel cost charges (if applicable), remaining balance, and payments applied — plus the two-part unbundled breakdown under Module F1.2.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What are the components of "Retail Supplier Charges" on a bill?
faqs.answer: Generation Charge, Supplier's Charge, WESM Charges (if applicable), Arrears (if any), and Interest or penalty charges (if any).

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What are the ERC-approved "pass-through" components related to Distribution and Transmission?
faqs.answer: Transmission Charge, Distribution Charge, Metering Charge, System Loss Charge, Local Franchise Tax, Real Property Tax, Senior Citizen Subsidy, Lifeline Rate Subsidy, VAT, Universal Charge, FIT-All Charge, Reinvestment Fund for Sustainable CAPEX Charge (if applicable), Arrears, and other ERC-approved government charges.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: How is the "Total Electricity Bill" computed under the Omnibus Rules?
faqs.answer: Total Electricity Bill = Retail Supplier Charges (component "a") + ERC-Approved Distribution/Transmission-Related Charges (component "b").

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What must a bill contain besides the charge breakdown?
faqs.answer: The Retail Supplier's customer-service contact details; the address, phone, and email of the ERC's Consumer Affairs Service (CAS); the NSP's customer-service and emergency numbers; and any other ERC-required announcements.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: How does billing flow from the NSP to the end customer?
faqs.answer: The NSP sends its billing statement to the Retail Supplier (or nominated Primary Retail Supplier) after providing meter reading data to the CRB; the Retail Supplier/Primary Retail Supplier then sends the consolidated bill to the Retail Customer within the timeframe specified in the RSC.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What if a Retail Customer has multiple Retail Suppliers?
faqs.answer: It receives one consolidated bill from the Primary Retail Supplier (covering NSP-approved wheeling charges) plus separate bills from each of its other Retail Suppliers for their respective Retail Supplier Charges.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Is a Retail Customer responsible for amounts its supplier fails to pay to other market participants?
faqs.answer: No — the customer is only responsible for amounts based on charges clearly identified in its RSC. If it is prejudiced by its supplier's non-payment to other participants, it may claim damages/indemnification under the RSC's breach-of-contract provisions.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier charge an administrative fee for collecting distribution/transmission charges?
faqs.answer: No — these pass-through charges are collected merely as a collecting agent on behalf of the NSP and do not form part of the Retail Supplier's revenue or losses, so no additional administrative fee may be added for collecting them.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Within what timeframe must a Retail Supplier pay amounts due to the NSP?
faqs.answer: Within the timeframe specified in their wheeling or transmission service agreement, to avoid disconnection of supply.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What must a Retail Supplier do with FIT-All charges it collects?
faqs.answer: Remit them to the FIT-All Fund Administrator, along with other ERC-approved pass-through charges, in line with Module C11.1(i).

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier impose late payment charges?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only if the terms are clearly stated in the RSC and previously disclosed to the Retail Customer; the same applies to bounced-check fees and related administrative fees.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What if late payment charges are not disclosed in the RSC?
faqs.answer: No late payment charges or administrative fees may be collected at all if they were not clearly stated in the RSC and previously disclosed to the customer.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: How must energy consumption charges under Aggregation (RAP) be billed?
faqs.answer: Module F on Billing and Payments applies equally to RAP. For Aggregation through a Virtual Meter in the WESM, each Aggregated Member receives its own billing statement reflecting its respective share of wheeling charges.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier disconnect an entire Aggregated Group over one member's non-payment?
faqs.answer: No — the Retail Supplier cannot request disconnection of the whole Aggregated Group due to one member's non-payment, though it may still enforce other remedies available under the RSC against the specific defaulting member.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What billing rules apply to a CREM End-user Redistributor (e.g., mall or condo) billing its tenants/unit-owners?
faqs.answer: It must bill individual unit-owners/users monthly, in a transparent manner mirroring the ERC-approved unbundled bill format, based only on actual consumption reflected in their sub-meters, without deriving any profit from the recovery of common-area or non-technical losses.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Are there rules on the format and legibility of a bill?
faqs.answer: Yes — bills must be in clear and simple language and must not use print sized or styled in a way that materially impairs legibility, similar to the standard applied to marketing/advertising materials.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Who sets the billing cycle for a Retail Customer?
faqs.answer: The Retail Supplier, DU, or SOLR defines a "Billing Cycle" — the period bound by start and end dates used to determine service usage for billing purposes — generally reflected in the RSC or applicable contract.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What obligations does a Retail Supplier have if it is also the collecting party for a DWSA?
faqs.answer: It must contract directly with the NSP for wheeling/transmission services and remains responsible for settling those charges with the NSP, separate from its own supplier charges owed by the customer.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: Are billing disputes handled differently for Retail Customers versus Captive Customers?
faqs.answer: Largely no — disputes over deficient bill deposits, for example, are treated the same as captive-customer disputes under DSOAR and other related ERC issuances, ensuring consistent consumer protection standards.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What rights does a customer have if it disagrees with a specific charge on its bill?
faqs.answer: It may exercise its Right to Payment Under Protest (Module M12), continuing to pay the undisputed portion to avoid disconnection while formally disputing the specific charge through the supplier's Complaint Handling Procedures or before the ERC.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: How are Universal Charges billed and remitted under the Customer Choice Programs?
faqs.answer: Universal charges continue to be billed and collected by the DU through the Retail Supplier and must be remitted to PSALM within fifteen (15) calendar days of the DU's collection. For DCCs qualified as Retail Customers, TransCo (or its buyer/concessionaire) bills and collects these directly.

faqs.section_title: Billing and Payments
faqs.question: What happens to over- or under-recoveries in regulated charges when a customer switches from captive to retail?
faqs.answer: Any over/under recovery in generation, transmission, system loss, lifeline subsidy, business tax, and senior citizen discount charges from when the customer was still captive is confirmed by the ERC and refunded/collected through the DU's bill, itemized as a separate line via the Retail Supplier currently serving the customer. 7. Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What entities are allowed to act as a SOLR?
faqs.answer: (a) a DU with an ERC-approved Business Separation and Unbundling Plan (BSUP) for regulated retail service, operating only within its own Franchise Area; and (b) a RES with a valid license and an ERC-approved BSUP for regulated retail service.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What must an entity have before it can be designated as a SOLR?
faqs.answer: WESM registration and membership; a Certificate of Compliance with WESM metering, prudential, and financial-obligation requirements; existing Retail Customers; and an ERC-approved BSUP for a Regulated Supply Business Segment.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: How long does the ERC take to issue a Letter of Designation to act as SOLR?
faqs.answer: Within sixty (60) calendar days from receipt of complete requirements, following submission of a letter of intent and proof of compliance with SOLR qualifications.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What is the purpose of a Last Resort Supply Event (LRSE)?
faqs.answer: An LRSE identifies circumstances under which a Retail Customer, no longer supplied by its chosen Retail Supplier, is entitled to backstop electricity service from a SOLR until it can arrange a new Retail Supplier.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: Can you list some of the circumstances considered an LRSE?
faqs.answer: Termination of the RSC due to breach not caused by the customer; termination of the TSA/DWSA between the supplier and NSP; the supplier ceasing operations; revocation of a GEOP Operating Permit; loss of WESM trading rights; a supplier's notice that it will stop supplying; unjust unilateral termination by the supplier; failure to continue service after a customer relocation; default in an RSC with an Aggregated Group; and revocation of the RES License or Letter-authority.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: Can the ERC recognize other circumstances as an LRSE beyond the enumerated list?
faqs.answer: Yes — any other circumstance the ERC deems an LRSE, upon the Retail Supplier's letter-request with supporting information/documents for the ERC's consideration.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: Can a customer disconnected for pilferage immediately avail of Last Resort Supply?
faqs.answer: No — a Retail Customer disconnected for pilferage by a Retail Supplier or RMSP cannot avail of Last Resort Supply unless it first pays in full all amounts due (including applicable charges) to the Retail Supplier or NSP.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What must a Retail Supplier do immediately upon discovering an LRSE?
faqs.answer: Immediately notify the affected Retail Customer(s), the CRB, and the ERC, including relevant supporting documents. Failure to notify is itself a violation subject to fines and penalties.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: How quickly must a Retail Customer decide whether to avail of Last Resort Supply?
faqs.answer: Within one (1) business day after being notified of the LRSE, informing the CRB of its decision.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What happens once the CRB is notified that a customer wants Last Resort Supply?
faqs.answer: The CRB, within one business day, sends notice to all SOLRs (Retail Suppliers acting as SOLR and the local DU-SOLR); the notified SOLRs then, through the CRB, present the customer their offer (effective transfer date, contract terms, right to later switch) within one further business day.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What must a customer do to formally accept a SOLR's offer?
faqs.answer: Sign the SOLR contract and pay the corresponding cash security deposit.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: Who remains responsible for energy used between a supplier's cessation/revocation and the effective SOLR switch?
faqs.answer: The Retail Supplier that caused the LRSE remains responsible for the energy consumed during that gap period, until the switch to SOLR takes effect.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What happens if a customer decides not to avail of Last Resort Supply?
faqs.answer: The CRB informs the NSP within one business day, and the NSP issues a 48-hour disconnection notice; if the customer fails to find a new Retail Supplier within that 48-hour window, the RMSP/NSP must disconnect it, unless the customer proves it is actively negotiating a new contract.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: When can a disconnected customer be reconnected after opting out of SOLR service?
faqs.answer: Only once it has entered into a contract with a new Retail Supplier.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What customer information does the CRB give to a SOLR taking on a new customer?
faqs.answer: Billing/service address, account number, meter reading date/cycle, billing date/cycle, meter number, DU rate class/subclass, usage measurement type, and the most recent twelve (12) months of historical usage.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: How much cash security deposit does a SOLR collect, and how must it be held?
faqs.answer: One (1) month's total estimated billing, based on the average of the previous six months' demand and energy usage, deposited in an escrow, restricted account, or Hold-out Agreement facility unavailable for the SOLR's working capital.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What happens to a SOLR deposit when a customer leaves SOLR service?
faqs.answer: The final SOLR bill is offset against the deposit (whether the customer transfers to a new supplier, reverts to Captive Market, or is terminated for nonpayment); any remaining balance and interest earned is refunded within thirty (30) calendar days (or a shorter agreed period) from the final meter reading date.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: How quickly must a SOLR submit a switch request once a contract is signed?
faqs.answer: Within one (1) business day of signing and deposit payment; the RMSP then conducts a special meter reading within one business day of receiving the SOLR's request.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What determines the "commencement date" of Last Resort Supply?
faqs.answer: The date of the Final Meter Reading marks the commencement date of Last Resort Supply.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What premium does a SOLR add to the energy price it charges?
faqs.answer: A five percent (5%) premium over the applicable WESM nodal energy price or bilateral contract price, to cover incremental administrative and overhead expenses — shown separately on the bill.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What items must appear on every SOLR bill?
faqs.answer: Energy consumed (with the 5% premium indicated separately); last approved unbundled supply charge and pass-through wheeling/system-loss/metering charges; Universal Charge; FIT-All; taxes; previous balance; billing period; issue date; meter readings and dates; meter serial/company number; SOLR contact information; and the ERC's customer hotline and website.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: What happens if a Retail Customer fails to pay its SOLR bill?
faqs.answer: The SOLR sends a 48-hour written disconnection notice; if unpaid after 48 hours, the SOLR informs the CRB, which forwards the disconnection request to the RMSP for execution within twenty-four (24) hours; reconnection occurs only after the customer settles all obligations.

faqs.section_title: Supplier of Last Resort (SOLR)
faqs.question: How long does a SOLR contract last, and does it auto-renew?
faqs.answer: It commences on the effective switch date and runs to the end of that Billing Cycle. If the customer does not transfer away by then, it is automatically renewed; the customer must give written notice at the start of a new Billing Cycle if it no longer wants Last Resort Supply, with non-renewal applying to the next cycle.
