faqs.answer: MERALCO noted that once a meter type is approved by the National Telecommunications Commission and the ERC, procurement of meters typically takes at least eighteen (18) months given CSP (Competitive Selection Process) guidelines, which could affect how quickly smaller customers can actually switch.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What did RESA (the Retail Electricity Suppliers Association) recommend regarding timing?
faqs.answer: RESA recommended a reasonable transition period rather than immediate effectivity, so DUs and Electric Cooperatives could scale up RCOA-compliant meter deployment, manage supply-demand impacts, renegotiate power supply agreements, and adjust billing cycles and financial flows.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What did CEPALCO specifically propose for the Mindanao grid?
faqs.answer: CEPALCO proposed an "Operational Readiness Criteria" (ORC) — a measurable checklist (covering AMI adoption and a stranded-contract mitigation/recovery plan) that should be satisfied island-by-island before activating the lower threshold, suggesting Luzon go first, then Visayas, then Mindanao only once each meets the ORC.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: How did the ERC respond to concerns about Mindanao's readiness specifically?
faqs.answer: The Commission acknowledged the concern, noted it is preparing a roadmap for threshold reduction anchored on readiness considerations rather than fixed timelines for Mindanao, and requested that stakeholders provide operational data to help guide the transition; any stranded-contract mitigation plan may require further refinements to the Omnibus Rules.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What deadline must a RES meet to start marketing to newly eligible 100kW–499kW end-users?
faqs.answer: Any ERC-licensed RES may conduct marketing activities to end-users already meeting the 100 kW to 499 kW threshold, or facilitate Aggregated Groups, based on demand eligibility effective from the Resolution's issuance — with submission of the switch Letter of Intent (LOI) required on or before 30 January 2026.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What happens to end-users or Aggregated Groups that fail to submit their Letter of Intent by 30 January 2026?
faqs.answer: They will not be allowed to switch on the target date of 26 June 2026; however, those unable to meet that deadline may still file an LOI between 31 January 2026 and 26 June 2026, provided their target switch date is not less than ninety (90) calendar days from 26 June 2026.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What is the general rule for target switch dates under all LOIs filed for the 100kW threshold?
faqs.answer: Every LOI to switch under the new 100 kW minimum threshold — whether for CREM/RCOA or RAP — must have a target switch date of not less than ninety (90) calendar days from the date the Network Service Provider (NSP) receives the LOI.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What deadline applies to DUs acting as RMSPs for registering with the CRB?
faqs.answer: All DUs operating where the WESM is functional must register as an RMSP with the Central Registration Body (CRB) on or before 30 December 2025.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: By when must an RMSP replace or enhance metering facilities for a newly eligible end-user under the lowered threshold?
faqs.answer: Not later than thirty (30) calendar days before the target switch date of 26 June 2026, for end-users or Aggregated Group members who submitted their LOI on or before 30 January 2026 — giving the CRB sufficient time to process the switch request.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: Can a DU file a separate CAPEX application to fund the metering rollout for the lowered threshold?
faqs.answer: Yes — the DU acting as RMSP may file a separate CAPEX application specifically for the procurement of the appropriate metering facilities needed to serve the newly eligible customer segment.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What ongoing obligation do DUs (as NSPs) have under the Resolution regarding customer notification?
faqs.answer: They must continuously comply with the notification requirement under Module D of the Omnibus Rules — i.e., informing eligible end-users on their monthly bill once their demand meets the applicable threshold.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What must the CRB do to prepare its systems for the surge in eligible customers?
faqs.answer: Ensure operationalization of all Customer Choice Programs and implement measures — including enhancement of its Central Registration and Settlement System (CRSS) — to handle an increased volume of Retail Customer registrations, with enhancements aligned with WESM Rules and the Retail Manual taking effect not later than 26 June 2026.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What other major regulatory issuance did the Commission commit to alongside Resolution No. 22?
faqs.answer: Amended Rules Governing the Implementation of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) Systems by Distribution Utilities, to provide the cost-recovery mechanism for metering facilities across the various customer choice and demand-management programs.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What broader planning document did the ERC commit to preparing under paragraph 5 of Resolution No. 22?
faqs.answer: A Comprehensive Roadmap for implementing the Customer Choice Programs in the Retail Market, including a complete market assessment, to help retail market participants prepare for further lowering of the threshold down to household levels.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: Does Resolution No. 22 affect implementation of Customer Choice Programs in BARMM?
faqs.answer: No — per paragraph 6, implementation of all Customer Choice Programs in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) remains within the authority and discretion of the BARMM government, not automatically imposed by the ERC's Resolution.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: Can end-users still switch under the old 500 kW threshold rules before the 100 kW threshold takes effect?
faqs.answer: Yes — per paragraph 7, prior to 26 June 2026, all end-users and Aggregated Groups meeting the existing 500 kW threshold under Module D of the Omnibus Rules may continue switching under the existing Module E procedures and requirements.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: Can a customer participate in both a Customer Choice Program and a demand-management program like Net-Metering at the same time?

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: Does the lower threshold mean participation in the Retail Market becomes mandatory for qualifying customers?
faqs.answer: No — the ERC explicitly reaffirmed, in response to stakeholder questions, that participation under RCOA remains voluntary even after the eligibility threshold is lowered to 100 kW.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What concern did FGEN Group raise about a "phased" approach, and how did the ERC respond?
faqs.answer: FGEN suggested lowering the threshold gradually (e.g., a half-way step at 300 kW for two to three years) to allow MSP/NSP technical readiness milestones to be met first; the ERC acknowledged the importance of MSP/NSP readiness and said it would consider a phased approach subject to readiness assessment results.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What did Aboitiz Power Corporation ask about facilities under RAP that exceed 100 kW once the new threshold applies?
faqs.answer: They sought clarification on whether such facilities would automatically be required to switch into RCOA upon expiry of their RAP contracts; the ERC noted the request for clarification but emphasized participation under RCOA remains voluntary.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What transitional period did Aboitiz Power propose in its comments (though not necessarily adopted verbatim)?
faqs.answer: A one-year preparatory period before the Resolution's effectivity, plus a ninety-day period for DUs to process switch requests once implementation begins, with customer meters procurable and ownable by either the customer or the DU.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: How did the ERC generally respond to the recurring theme of "insufficient transition time" in stakeholder comments?
faqs.answer: The Commission consistently acknowledged that a phased or transitional approach may be necessary given complexities in metering deployment, and indicated it would coordinate with the DOE, IEMOP, and other stakeholders to align implementation timelines with actual technical and administrative readiness.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: What happens if a provision of Resolution No. 22 is later declared invalid?
faqs.answer: Per its own separability clause (paragraph 11), the other unaffected parts or provisions of the Resolution remain in full force and effect.

faqs.section_title: Resolution No. 22, Series of 2025 — Lowering the Eligibility Threshold to 100kW
faqs.question: Why does this lower threshold matter so much for smaller commercial and industrial customers?
faqs.answer: It effectively opens up the competitive Retail Market to a much larger pool of mid-sized commercial and industrial electricity users (previously locked at 500 kW and above), giving them the same rights to shop for suppliers, negotiate rates, and potentially realize cost savings that only larger 1 MW+ customers previously enjoyed.

Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: If a Retail Customer has multiple Retail Suppliers, who actually deals with the DU and the CRB day-to-day?
faqs.answer: The Primary Retail Supplier, nominated in writing by the customer, serves as the single point of contact for the CRB and all NSPs, is responsible for billing/collecting NSP charges, and is the only supplier allowed to execute the DWSA with the DU on the customer's behalf.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How does a Retail Customer protect itself against a Retail Supplier that fails to remit distribution/transmission charges to the DU?
faqs.answer: Since these are pass-through charges collected merely as a collecting agent, the customer is not liable for the supplier's non-payment to the DU; however, the customer should ensure the RSC contains clear breach-of-contract and indemnification provisions to claim damages if it is prejudiced (e.g., by a resulting disconnection dispute).

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What is the practical difference between an LRSE under Module G3.2(a)-(i) versus (j)-(k)?
faqs.answer: LRSEs (a) through (i) are self-executing once the CRB confirms occurrence and the customer opts for SOLR — no ERC confirmation needed. LRSEs (j) (ERC revocation of license) and (k) (other ERC-recognized circumstances) require the CRB to first receive notice of the revocation or ERC confirmation before the same procedures apply.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why might a Retail Customer prefer a fixed-price RSC over an indexed or Time-of-Use (TOU) pricing structure?
faqs.answer: A fixed price offers budget certainty and insulation from WESM price volatility, while indexed or TOU pricing can offer potential savings if the customer's consumption profile aligns well with off-peak periods, but exposes it to market price swings — the choice depends on the customer's risk appetite and load profile.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier legally require a customer to also buy value-added services (e.g., energy audits) as a condition of the RSC?
faqs.answer: The Omnibus Rules do not prohibit bundling value-added services, but any related charges must be clearly disclosed and stated in the RSC beforehand (Module L12.2(d)) — undisclosed bundled charges would violate the disclosure and marketing-conduct rules.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What is the interplay between the Cooling-off Period and the requirement that supply commence only after that period expires?
faqs.answer: The RSC cannot start supply before the Cooling-off Period lapses (unless both parties agree otherwise), which effectively means a customer's right to walk away penalty-free is preserved throughout the entire pre-supply window, not just on paper.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: If a Retail Customer wants to dispute a bill but also avoid disconnection, what is the correct procedure?
faqs.answer: It should invoke its Right to Payment Under Protest (Module M12) — paying the undisputed or full amount while formally raising the dispute through the Complaint Handling Procedures — since simply withholding payment could expose it to a valid disconnection notice.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How does the ERC prevent a DU's Local RES from gaining an unfair information advantage over competing RES?
faqs.answer: Through Module L14's strict operational-separation rules — a DU cannot share distribution-system information, joint marketing, or preferential access with its Local/Affiliate RES unless the same information/access is equally available to all other Retail Suppliers on the same terms.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why does the 50% cap on affiliate-generation sourcing (Module C12.4) matter for market competition?
faqs.answer: It prevents a Retail Supplier from becoming a mere captive off-taker of its own affiliated generator, ensuring it still sources a meaningful share of its supply competitively from the broader market, which helps maintain genuine price discovery and competition.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How does the Retail Supplier Scorecard's heavy weighting toward "zero ERC Decisions" (25%, all-or-nothing) shape supplier behavior?
faqs.answer: It creates a strong incentive for suppliers to avoid escalation of any dispute all the way to a formal ERC Decision, since even a single adverse decision costs the supplier the entire 25% weight, likely pushing its Total Rating toward "Satisfactory" or "Failed" rather than "Very Satisfactory."

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: If a customer's demand drops below threshold only briefly due to a seasonal dip, can it still revert to captive status?
faqs.answer: No — Module K1.1 requires the drop below 25% of the CREM threshold to persist for six consecutive months and not be attributable to seasonal demand; a short seasonal dip would not qualify the customer for reversion.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What is the legal effect of an Aggregated Group member remaining part of the group even after being disconnected for pilferage?
faqs.answer: The individual erring member is disconnected, but the Aggregated Group itself (as recognized by the CRB) continues to exist and its RSC remains valid for the remaining, non-erring members — protecting the group's aggregated eligibility status.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier bill a Retail Customer for costs the customer never agreed to in writing?
faqs.answer: No — under Module L12.7, rates and terms may only be modified by written agreement of both parties; any new charge not disclosed and agreed to in the RSC (or a written amendment) cannot lawfully be billed.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: If a Retail Supplier ceases operations, what is the maximum exposure a Retail Customer faces before securing new supply?
faqs.answer: The defaulting supplier remains liable for continuous supply until the customer's switch to a new Retail Supplier or SOLR is effective; if the resulting SOLR/new rate is higher, the customer may seek indemnification under the RSC's remedy provisions — so exposure is contractually, not statutorily, capped.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How does the interplay of Module D6 (metering) and Module E (switching) create a practical bottleneck for smaller customers?
faqs.answer: Since RMSPs have thirty (extendable to sixty) days to install/upgrade metering after a switch notice, and the customer must also complete a ninety-day NSP notice period, actual switch timelines can realistically stretch to several months, which is precisely the readiness concern stakeholders raised about the lowered 100 kW threshold.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why does the Omnibus Rules require a Retail Supplier's PSAs to be available for ERC review even though PSAs are private commercial contracts?
faqs.answer: To verify that fuel-cost pass-through structures and pricing were negotiated at arm's length, preventing affiliate self-dealing or anti-competitive collusion that could otherwise be hidden behind commercially "confidential" contract terms.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What is the significance of the RSC's liberal-construction-in-favor-of-the-customer rule (Module L12.11)?
faqs.answer: For templated (non-negotiated) contracts, any genuine ambiguity is resolved against the drafter (the Retail Supplier) — mirroring the classic "contra proferentem" principle in contract law and giving customers an interpretive advantage in disputes over unclear RSC language.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How should a company evaluate whether joining RAP makes more sense than waiting to individually qualify for CREM?
faqs.answer: RAP lets a company access retail competition and potential savings sooner (if its own demand is below threshold), but it must accept aggregation-specific constraints (e.g., no unilateral opt-out mid-contract, dependence on the aggregator's performance) — a trade-off between earlier market access and reduced individual flexibility.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why might the lowering of the eligibility threshold to 100kW increase — rather than decrease — near-term system risk, according to stakeholders?
faqs.answer: Because it dramatically increases the volume of customers requiring interval-capable meters and CRB processing capacity almost simultaneously, and if AMI deployment, RMSP capacity, and CRSS system enhancements lag behind, the resulting switching backlog or billing errors could undermine confidence in the newly expanded Retail Market.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What compliance risk does a Retail Supplier face if it under-reports complaint data to the ERC?
faqs.answer: Beyond the direct scoring impact (poor Completeness/Timeliness scores under Module O), under-reporting is itself a violation subject to fines and penalties, and could separately trigger a Show-Cause Order — compounding the damage to its Good Standing rating on two fronts at once.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How does the "no cross-subsidization" principle appear in more than one part of the Omnibus Rules?
faqs.answer: It recurs in metering-cost allocation (Module D6.4 — no captive-customer subsidy of Retail Customer metering costs), business unbundling (Module C11.1(a) and L14 — no cross-subsidy between a DU's regulated and non-regulated businesses), and DU financing restrictions on its Affiliate RES (Module L14.10-11) — reflecting a consistent regulatory theme against hidden subsidies distorting competition.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why does the Omnibus Rules distinguish between "Local RES" and ordinary "RES" so carefully?
faqs.answer: Because a Local RES is inherently affiliated with the DU controlling the wires in its franchise area, creating a structural conflict-of-interest risk; the extra safeguards (Letter-authority instead of full license, mandatory distinguishing branding, strict information-sharing bans) exist specifically to police that built-in conflict.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How does a customer verify that a company claiming to be a "licensed RES" is legitimate?
faqs.answer: By checking the ERC's official website for the current list of licensed RES and authorized Local RES — DUs are specifically barred from offering opinions on suppliers and must direct such inquiries to the ERC website rather than vouching for any supplier themselves.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What happens, procedurally, if both the Retail Supplier and the Retail Customer disagree on whether a valid LRSE occurred?
faqs.answer: Since notification and CRB processing under Module G4 proceed largely on the Retail Supplier's notice, a customer disputing the existence or cause of an LRSE would need to pursue that disagreement through the Complaint Handling Procedures and, if unresolved, before the ERC, without that dispute necessarily halting the SOLR transition itself.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Does a customer lose its accumulated rights (e.g., historical usage records) when it switches between Retail Suppliers?
faqs.answer: No — the customer's Right to Information (Module M7) entitles it to obtain its own historical metered quantities and consumption data free of charge from any Retail Supplier, and the CRB/NSP retain and can supply twelve months of historical usage data to a new supplier or SOLR as needed.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How does the ERC balance encouraging switching (competition) against protecting suppliers from opportunistic "hop-and-drop" customers?
faqs.answer: Through provisions like the Cooling-off waiver, disclosed early-termination charges (Module L12.2(i)), and the requirement that outstanding lawful obligations to the prior supplier survive a regular switch (Module E1.4) — customers can switch, but cannot simply walk away from legitimate contractual obligations by doing so.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What is the ultimate regulatory rationale for requiring Retail Suppliers to unbundle their charges on every bill?
faqs.answer: Unbundling (Module F1.2) lets customers see exactly what portion of their bill is the supplier's own charge versus pass-through NSP/government charges, enabling meaningful price comparison between suppliers and preventing suppliers from disguising markups within opaque bundled rates.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why would a large industrial customer with stable, continuous (baseload) consumption typically be more attractive to Retail Suppliers than a customer with volatile demand?
faqs.answer: A stable baseload profile is easier and cheaper to hedge or match against WESM/PSA supply, reducing the supplier's balancing risk and cost — which is also why the ARMAR reports typically show industrial CREM customers achieving higher load factors and larger absolute cost savings than commercial customers.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Can a Retail Supplier refuse to serve a customer that meets all eligibility and documentary requirements?
faqs.answer: The Omnibus Rules do not impose a "universal service" obligation on ordinary Retail Suppliers (unlike SOLRs); however, if a supplier engages in unjustified selective refusal in a way that constitutes anti-competitive or discriminatory conduct, this could expose it to ERC sanctions under Module A2.1(e)'s consumer-protection objectives.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What happens if an Aggregated Group's Retail Supplier and one member disagree on whether an "act of default" occurred?
faqs.answer: The affected member/group may pursue termination and reversion to the Captive Market under Module K3.2-K3.4, but if the supplier disputes the existence of a default, the matter would proceed through the Complaint Handling Procedures and potentially an ERC Dispute Resolution Case, with the supplier still obligated to continue supply in the interim.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: How should a beginner analyst read the ARMAR alongside the Omnibus Rules to build a complete picture of the Retail Market?
faqs.answer: The Omnibus Rules explain the legal rights, obligations, and procedures that govern the market, while the ARMAR shows how those rules actually play out in practice — participation levels, pricing, competition, and consumer benefits — together forming the "rules" and "results" halves of understanding the market.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why might market concentration (HHI/C4) remain a concern even as the eligibility threshold falls to 100kW?
faqs.answer: A lower threshold increases the number of participants but does not automatically diversify supplier market share; if the same large corporate groups (e.g., MERALCO Group, Aboitiz Group) simply absorb most of the newly eligible customers, concentration indices could remain elevated even as headline participation numbers grow.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What is the relationship between the SOLR's "5% premium" and the incentive for customers to quickly find a new Retail Supplier?
faqs.answer: Because Last Resort Supply is deliberately priced at a premium over market rates and is meant to be temporary, this pricing structure discourages customers from indefinitely staying on SOLR service and instead nudges them to actively negotiate a new RSC as soon as practicable.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why does the Omnibus Rules require Retail Suppliers to submit an annual training report to the ERC?
faqs.answer: Because sales staff conduct is imputed to the supplier itself (Module L1.3-1.4), the ERC uses training records and reports as a proactive compliance check — ensuring staff actually receive the product-knowledge and conduct training required under Module L7, rather than relying solely on after-the-fact complaint investigations.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: If a customer's building qualifies as a CREM End-user Redistributor but the homeowners' association fails to pass the required resolution before the RSC's expiry, what happens?
faqs.answer: Per the transitory provisions (Module

Q461. How do the escrow/restricted-account requirements for cash security deposits protect customers if a Retail Supplier goes bankrupt?
faqs.answer: Because the deposit must be held in a segregated escrow, restricted account, or Hold-out Agreement facility unavailable for the supplier's working capital, the funds are legally shielded from the supplier's general creditors in an insolvency scenario, unlike an ordinary unsecured deposit commingled with operating funds.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: Why is the distinction between "Contract Price" and "Electricity Price" important when comparing supplier offers?
faqs.answer: A supplier's advertised Contract Price only reflects its own generation/supply charge; the actual Electricity Price a customer pays also includes pass-through NSP and government charges that are largely the same regardless of supplier — so meaningful price comparisons should focus on the Contract Price component, not the full bill total.

faqs.section_title: Expert-Level Analysis — Cross-Cutting Issues and Practical Scenarios
faqs.question: What long-term policy direction does the combination of the Omnibus Rules and Resolution No. 22 suggest for the Philippine electricity sector?
faqs.answer: A steady, EPIRA-mandated march toward full retail competition — starting from 1 MW in 2013, dropping stepwise to 750 kW, 500 kW, and now 100 kW by mid-2026 — with an explicitly stated ultimate goal of eventually extending customer choice down to household demand levels. 21.
